title: Baron: faith in intellect by essence, yet belongs to will by origin, annexed act, fruits
source_text: VI. Similia docet Rob. Baronius Articulo supra citato. Quamvis enim numero quinto asserat fidem esse in solo intellectu proprie subjective, & respectu suae essentiae, idque quoniam omnes fidei partes, notitia, scilicet, assensus, & etiam, ipso judice, fiducia in intellectu consistunt; numero tamen septimo affirmat fidem ad voluntatem pertinere multis modis. Et primo quidem ratione originis: secundo, ratione actus annexi: tertio, ratione fructuum, qui ex fide in voluntate nascuntur. Quod postea explicans, Pertinet, inquit, ad eam ratione originis, quia intellectus noster sine voluntatis inclinatione, & imperio ad assentiendum movetur, & in captivitatem redigitur. Unde assensus fidei appellari solet actus imperatus a voluntate; item denominari solet voluntarius & liber actus; videlicet quia dependet a principio libere agente, hoc est, a voluntate; atque hinc est quod dixit Augustinus, Neminem credere nisi volentem. Pertinet etiam fides ad voluntatem ratione actus annexi & concomitantis; nam in eo ipso instanti, quo fides in intellectu assentitur Evangelicis promissionibus, easque certo & stabili judicio sibi applicat, voluntas ardenti amore gratiam & favorem Dei amplectitur. Denique pertinet ad eam, ratione fructuum & operationum, quia illuminationem fidei in mente sequitur sanctificatio & emollitio voluntatis.
pass_a_gloss: Robert Baron teaches similar things in the article cited above. Although in number five he asserts faith is in the intellect alone properly and subjectively and with respect to its essence — since all parts of faith (knowledge, assent, and even, by his judgment, trust) consist in the intellect — yet in number seven he affirms faith belongs to the will in many ways: first by reason of origin; second by reason of an annexed act; third by reason of fruits born from faith in the will. Explaining later: It belongs to the will by origin because our intellect is moved to assent without the will's inclination and command and is brought into captivity. Hence faith's assent is usually called an act commanded by the will, and a voluntary free act, because it depends on a freely acting principle, that is, the will; and hence Augustine said no one believes unless willing. Faith also belongs to the will by an annexed concomitant act: in the very instant intellect assents to Gospel promises and applies them with firm judgment, the will embraces God's grace and favor with ardent love. Finally it belongs by fruits and operations, because sanctification and softening of the will follow the illumination of faith in the mind.
pass_b_english: Baron: essence in intellect (even fiducia), yet faith touches will by origin, annexed love-act, and fruits.
Assent is often called will-commanded and free (Augustine: none believe unwilling); love co-instant; sanctification follows.

choices.why: Baron still seats fiducia in intellect while granting will-links.
